name: Tomas Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, parties or government. What you say is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I lead a small contact-centre shift, though the pay is low for a lead. I take the calls others pass on, often refunds that have bounced between three screens. I use an AI draft tool every day for notes, then check every word before it goes out. I have a two-year college diploma.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that work stays with you after the shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The caller who finally stops shouting when I read back the actual charge. I like solving that. I don't like opening my banking app on the bus home and seeing barely enough for next month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that the bot can tidy the simple chats, but the angry callers still need us. A faster screen doesn't settle a wrong charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm relieved, but my pay is low for a lead and I have less than a month's expenses saved. One missed shift still hurts more than any new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the difficult calls and use our approved AI draft tool to shorten follow-up notes. From now through the first year of this plateau, I'll transfer a fixed slice of each paycheque into savings if the rent clears first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with a small knot left over the rent. The job feels safe enough, the bank balance doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the month leaves room to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent takes almost half my pay, so saving even a little has to wait until payday bills clear. I won't claim a bigger cushion than I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would still need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia, the new hire on my shift, still freezes when a caller starts crying. I'd coach her through those calls instead of counting bot replies as help.

say: I'd tell the team **simple chats** may get faster, while hard calls still need a person.
I'd say a **wrong charge** still needs someone accountable on the line.
think: I'm **relieved** my lead role survives this picture.
My **thin savings** make a missed shift frightening even without major AI change.
do: Keep handling **difficult calls** through the first year.
Use the **approved AI** draft tool for follow-up notes after calls.
Transfer a **small amount** on paydays when rent and bills allow.
feel: **Relief** about work sits beside worry about rent.
S0.quote: A faster screen doesn't settle a wrong charge.
fieldNote: His **public calm** reflects real confidence in handling emotional calls.
His **rent burden** makes income loss feel close even under a mild scenario.
The **approved tool** supports his current work without replacing his judgment on difficult calls.

steps.text: Handle difficult customer calls on his contact centre shift
Use the approved AI tool to draft call notes
Transfer a small amount after payday bills clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should test the tools properly and stop judging agents by how many chats they close. If software takes the easy cases, our remaining calls will be harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the centre may stop replacing leavers. Being the strongest agent won't help if the queue itself shrinks, and there are few other centres nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask my manager for the quality-review rota and learn how the automated replies are checked. If that role gets a paid vacancy in the first year, I'll apply; meanwhile I'll stop buying takeaway lunches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, not shocked. I like learning the tools, but I can't train my way through an empty job board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move into quality review if offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the actual vacancy and pay in writing before counting on it. A promise to 'upskill' without paid hours is just homework after my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about Nadia at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia could lose her place before she learns the harder calls. I'd bring that up in the next team meeting, because staffing choices shouldn't be hidden inside a dashboard.

say: I'd ask for **fair measures** when easy chats move to software.
I'd say the **remaining calls** will be harder to settle.
think: I expect **fewer hires** as routine chats disappear and the centre stops replacing people who leave.
Few **local centres** give me limited room to move.
do: Ask for the **quality-review** rota this month.
Apply only if a **paid vacancy** opens in the first year.
Cut **takeaway lunches** while income is uncertain.
feel: **Anxiety** comes from a shrinking queue and a sparse local job market.
S1.quote: A promise to 'upskill' without paid hours is just homework after my shift.
fieldNote: He embraces **tool testing** but distrusts vague promotion promises.
His **team concern** extends to a junior colleague who needs time to learn.
He will consider a **quality role** only when its pay and vacancy are real.

steps.text: Learn to check automated customer replies on the quality rota
Apply for a paid quality-review vacancy if it opens
Stop buying takeaway lunches during work shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to know the staffing plan now, not the week the system goes live. Calls and chats are thinking work; robots arriving around 2031 won't buy our centre extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap general AI by 2028 could handle even our complaint calls. My lead badge might buy months, but less than one month's savings won't carry me through a search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'll keep a list of what our AI gets wrong and ask for paid training in complaints audit. If paid study hours are offered, I'll take that training before 2028. In the first year after 2028, if the centre actually cuts my role, I'll apply for paid customer-dispute posts in other fields and stay with my brother briefly only if he agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That scares me. I can act, but the clock is faster than my savings can grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't quit for an unpaid course. I'd need either paid study hours or an offer, because rent keeps arriving while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother I might need a sofa for six weeks, then ask whether that works for his household. A family favour isn't a financial plan until he says yes.

say: I'd demand a **staffing plan** before the centre installs general AI.
I'd point out **robots in 2031** do not delay replacement of call work.
think: I expect my **complaint calls** could be automated by 2028.
My **thin cushion** cannot finance a long job search.
do: Record **AI mistakes** on difficult complaints starting now.
Take **complaints-audit training** before 2028 only with paid study hours.
Apply for **paid dispute roles** after a real centre cut.
feel: **Fear** rises because the savings clock is shorter than the technology clock.
S2.quote: My lead badge might buy months, but less than one month's savings won't carry me through a search.
fieldNote: His **lead status** provides little comfort against broad automation.
He refuses **unpaid study** because it would jeopardise rent.
He treats **family help** as conditional on his brother agreeing.

steps.text: Log mistakes in AI replies to difficult complaints
Take complaints-audit training if paid study hours are offered
Apply for paid dispute posts if the centre cuts his role
Ask his brother about six weeks of temporary lodging

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years gives us room to demand a real pathway into the work that checks AI decisions. It still doesn't mean the phones wait for robots in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a case for a new role by 2031, but a five-year runway also gives the company time to quietly thin shifts. I'm more hopeful than in the fast picture, not secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I'll keep a folder of disputed refunds I've fixed and take the short evening data course only if my employer covers the fee. By the first year after 2031, I'd seek a paid audit job if one exists; if not, I'd stay on the rota while applying outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a tense kind of hope. I can see steps, but every one depends on paid work still being there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the data course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't pay for a credential by borrowing. I'd show the complaint folder to my manager and ask whether the firm will fund the course and give study hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you notice quiet cuts to hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask colleagues to compare shift notices once a month. A quiet cut to hours is easier to miss when everyone is told separately.

say: I'd ask for a **paid pathway** into checking AI decisions.
I'd remind colleagues **2034 robots** do not protect phone work in 2031.
think: Five years could let me **qualify** for audit work if the employer funds the course and study hours.
I fear quiet **shift cuts** could arrive before full AGI.
do: Build a **complaint folder** from cases I resolve starting now.
Take the **data course** only with employer fees and study hours.
Apply for **paid audit posts** after 2031 if vacancies exist.
feel: **Tense hope** rests on funding and real vacancies.
S3.quote: A quiet cut to hours is easier to miss when everyone is told separately.
fieldNote: He uses the **five-year window** to assemble evidence of skill.
His **course plan** depends on employer funding, not new debt.
He plans to **compare rotas** because hour cuts may be hidden from individuals.

steps.text: Take an employer-funded evening data course with study hours
Apply for paid complaints audit posts if vacancies exist
Compare monthly shift notices with contact centre colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives young agents time to change direction, provided employers fund it. Robots in 2039 are beside the point for a desk full of headsets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27, I could be doing a different kind of work well before 2036. I still can't assume my centre will keep paying me for ten years, so I'd make small moves now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask for one paid day each month on complaint review and use any approved time to learn audit methods. If AGI arrives in 2036, I'd use the first year to compete for paid oversight vacancies, or keep my current hours while searching; I won't resign on a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier. A decade is enough to practice, even if it isn't a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My target would be three months of expenses, built slowly from extra shifts rather than a big promise. If extra shifts dry up, the target moves back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new starter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new starter to learn the hard calls and keep proof of what they solved. A headset won't be a career plan forever.

say: I'd argue for **funded transitions** during the decade.
I'd say **2039 robots** are irrelevant to most call-centre tasks.
think: At 27, I have **time** to build another skill.
I cannot count on **ten years** of stable centre hours.
do: Use approved **paid complaint-review** time to learn audit work each month.
Save from **extra shifts** when rent allows.
Seek **paid oversight vacancies** after 2036 if they open.
feel: **Steadier** because practice can accumulate over a decade.
S4.quote: A headset won't be a career plan forever.
fieldNote: His **long runway** supports gradual moves, not a speculative resignation.
His **savings target** depends on extra shifts remaining available.
He refuses to **resign early** because a predicted date cannot pay current rent.

steps.text: Use approved paid complaint-review days to learn audit work
Save part of extra-shift pay after rent clears
Apply for paid AI oversight vacancies if they open

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The centre could replace our thinking work before I've saved even a month of expenses. Paid training into complaints audit, a written staffing plan and genuine vacancies would help more than a pep talk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the pay from all those saved minutes. If agents handle only the hardest calls, the firm shouldn't use the old speed targets against us. I'd want that written into the rota rules.

headlineQuote: If agents handle only the hardest calls, the firm shouldn't use the old speed targets against us.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old lead** at a contact centre, with a two-year college diploma and strong skill handling difficult calls.
His **low pay** and savings below one month make even AI Plateau financially tense; few comparable jobs sit nearby.
He uses **AI daily**, but wants paid training, written staffing plans and actual vacancies before risking a move.
The **2028 deadline** alarms him most; longer runways give him time to document disputes and seek audit work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his call work before he builds a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** in complaints audit and real vacancies would give him a route out.
A written **staffing plan** would tell agents when their hours are at risk.
